deep.reconstruction:
There is no mathematical derivation on this page. It is a heavily corrected German prose draft, apparently part of an expert opinion (Gutachten) or letter. The previous page opens 'Hochverehrter Herr Professor', and the next page mentions Gen.-Lt. Baeyer and the Royal Hanoverian government. The context is Baeyer's proposal of the early 1860s for a Central European arc measurement (Mitteleuropäische Gradmessung) and whether Hanover should take part.

The argument runs as follows.
(1) Earlier determinations of the best-fitting ellipsoid chose its parameters so that the geodetic latitudes and longitudes of all arc measurements agreed as closely as possible with the astronomical ones. That is a least-squares minimisation of the deflections of the vertical (Lothabweichungen). In modern terms: minimise sum(xi_i^2 + eta_i^2), where xi = Phi_astro - phi_geod and eta = (Lambda_astro - lambda_geod)*cos(phi).
(2) Gauss had pointed out that such deflections are to be expected everywhere, not only near high mountains, because of the unevenness and non-uniform density of the crust. Airy and others then showed how strongly these deflections make all previous figure-of-the-earth determinations uncertain.
(3) Hence, in the reduction of the two newest great arcs, the English and the Russian (Struve) arcs, an attempt was made to compute the deflections from the shape of the surrounding terrain. Riemann refers to the reduction of all English arc measurements, undertaken at Airy's request and carried out in 1850-1858 by the Royal Engineers (the Ordnance Survey Principal Triangulation, published 1858). The local deflections at the stations were computed from the attraction of the visible topography, and Riemann reports how far they agreed with the computed values.
(4) This method cannot give the true values, because the unequal density of the underlying strata must be ignored.
(5) Riemann proposes that the deflections could be found far more accurately from variations in the intensity of gravity, measured by pendulum observations at a sufficient number of points. The Hanoverian arc measurement (Gauss's) could be completed after the fact by pendulum observations, as has been done for most older arc measurements, and such an investigation could then be carried out for it.

The implicit modern content (my addition, not on the page) is that the deflections are horizontal derivatives of the disturbing potential. They can be obtained from surface gravity anomalies by an integral formula, namely Stokes 1849 for geoid undulations and Vening Meinesz 1928 for the deflections themselves. Riemann states the idea only qualitatively and gives no formula.
errors: No mathematical errors, since there is no mathematics on the page.

Historical nuance: the first systematic computation of local attraction from terrain was Pratt's work on the Indian arc (1855). Pratt's result and Airy's 1855 isostasy paper are presumably the 'Untersuchungen von Airy u. A.'. Riemann's emphasis on the English and Russian arcs is accurate for the Ordnance Survey (Clarke/James 1858), which computed local attraction at Arthur's Seat and other stations from topography.

results.what: Determination of the best-fitting ellipsoid by least-squares minimisation of the differences between astronomical and geodetic coordinates (deflections of the vertical)
results.modern_name: Arc-measurement adjustment for the reference ellipsoid (e.g. Bessel 1841)
results.usually_credited_to: Bessel, Walbeck, Airy, Schmidt (first half of 19th century)

results.what: Computing local deflections of the vertical from the attraction of the surrounding topography
results.usually_credited_to: Pratt (1855), Ordnance Survey (Clarke & James, 1858); idea goes back to Bouguer and Maskelyne

results.what: Proposal to determine deflections of the vertical from gravity variations measured by pendulum at many points, to supplement the Hanoverian arc measurement
results.modern_name: Gravimetric determination of deflections of the vertical (Vening Meinesz formula; Stokes's gravimetric geodesy)
results.usually_credited_to: Stokes (1849) in principle; Vening Meinesz (1928) for the explicit deflection formula; Helmert later for practice

deep.surprise_reason: This is a non-mathematical administrative or scientific draft about geodesy. The suggestion to use pendulum gravity data to find deflections is qualitative and was in the air after Stokes (1849); Baeyer's programme itself included pendulum work. It is a mildly interesting document of Riemann's involvement in the Central European arc measurement, but it contains no new result.
transcription_corrections: Line 1: Riemann first wrote 'bestimmen' and replaced it with 'ermitteln' (written above). 'früheren Untersuchungen' is struck through and 'früheren' rewritten above 'Versuchen'.
Line 2: the interlinear insertion above 'Ellipsoid' looks like 'das durch Längengradmessungen geschaffene/gebildete' rather than 'das sich ergebende'; this reading is uncertain.

'Breitenabweichungen' in line 4: the first part ('Breiten'/'Loth') is struck and the line reads 'die Lothabweichungen des Lothes'. More precisely it should probably read 'die Lothabweichungen allenthalben möglichst klein werden'.
'vom Kön. engl. Ingenieurcorps' is correct and refers to the Royal Engineers / Ordnance Survey.

'fehlt sich dieser Unterschied[?]' is doubtful. The context suggests something like 'stellt sich dieser Unterschied ... heraus' or 'übereinstimmend gefunden worden'; the phrase is largely struck through.

The interlinear '{+nichtlich[?]+}' is more likely the struck 'Lichtstrahlen'/'nicht genau' fragments. The surviving sentence reads: 'Freilich konnte, da die ungleiche Dichtigkeit der unter dem Horizont liegenden Erdschichten ganz unberücksichtigt bleiben mußte, ihr Werth auf diesem Wege nicht gefunden werden.' 'Horizontlagenden' should probably read 'unter dem Horizont liegenden' or 'darunter liegenden' (uncertain).

'durch [-Pendel-]beobachtungen' in the 'Weit genauer' sentence: the struck word appears to be 'Pendel' in 'Pendelbeobachtungen', and the phrase reads 'aus den Variationen in der Intensität der Schwere ..., wenn diese in einer hinreichenden Anzahl von Punkten durch Pendelbeobachtungen ermittelt würde'.
The word above 'Pendelbeobachtungen' near the end is probably 'vervollständigt' or 'ergänzt'. The final line clearly reads 'durch Pendelbeobachtungen ergänzt würde'.
The folio number '126' in the right margin is the archival foliation, not Riemann's text.
